newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Somalia factions to discuss new national charter.
newsitem.headline: Somalia factions to discuss new national charter.

text.p: Somalia faction leader Ali Mahdi Mohammed said on Wednesday a new national charter would be the subject of a National Salvation Council (NSC) meeting to start on Thursday.
Mahdi told a news conference the eight-day meeting in the Ethiopia resort town of Sodere would set a date for a national reconciliation conference for all Somali factions in Bossaso.

Twenty-six Somali faction leaders agreed in Sodere last December to hold a national reconciliation conference, but faction leader Hussein Aideed and Mohamed Egal, president of the self-declared Somaliland Republic, boycotted the meeting.

"The Bossaso reconciliation conference will have the task of approving a national charter that leads to the establishment of a transitional government until a national election will be held," said Mahdi, one of five NSC chairmen. He added the NSC would discuss the charter on Thursday.
Mahdi said the reconciliation conference which should have been held in Bossaso on June 10 was delayed at Aideed's request.

"The Bossaso meeting was delayed because Aideed indicated that he wanted to join the peace process. He requested that we delay the reconciliation conference and since we wanted to give him a chance we agreed to postpone the session," he said.

A series of agreements between faction leaders this year have been undermined by slow implementation of specifics such as dismantling roadblocks and removing the Green Line that divides the Somali capital Mogadishu, a U.N. Somalia expert in Nairobi said.

Despite attempts at reconciliation, Aideed's militia occupied Bay, Bakool and Lower Shabelle regions, killing many and destroying property, Mahdi said. He demanded unconditional withdrawal of Aideed's troops.
NSC is mandated to draft a national charter and organise a national reocnciliation conference that leads toward establishment of a transitional government before elections are held.

Mahdi also labelled the Islamic fundamentalist group Al-Ittihad a terrorist front that aimed to destabilise the region and said Ethiopia played no role in a recent engagement against Al-Ittihad inside Somalia.
"The Somali National Front operating along the border with Ethiopia has informed us that they alone engaged Al-Ittihad forces and we have no reason to doubt their word," he said.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi warned last week his forces will hunt down Al-Ittihad, which it blames for bomb attacks in Ethiopia.

Somalia has lacked a central authority since the late president Siad Barre was overthrown in 1991. Civil war between Somali faction leaders compounded a famine in 1992/93 in which around 300,000 people died.
